title: Claims: True or False
objective: After this level you can explain what a claim is and why only claims, not questions or commands, can be true or false.
summary: A claim is a sentence that can be true or false, even a false one. Questions, commands and exclamations are neither, so they can't be premises or conclusions.

cards.headline: "Are you sleepy yet?" can't be true. It can't be false either.
cards.body: Try it: nobody answers a question with "False!" But reply "I'm not sleepy", and you've said something that is either true or false. That small difference decides what an argument can be built from.

cards.headline: What a claim is
cards.body: A claim, which logicians also call a statement, is a sentence that can be true or false. "The Nile is a river in northeastern Africa" is a claim, and a true one. "The Yangtze is a river in Japan" is a claim too, just a false one. Being wrong doesn't disqualify a sentence. It only has to be the kind of thing that could be right or wrong.

cards.headline: Questions, commands and ouches
cards.body: Three kinds of sentence can't be true or false. Questions: "Are you sleepy yet?" Commands: "Wake up!" Exclamations: "Ouch!" None of them states how things are, so none of them is a claim. Answer the question, though, and you're back in business. Questions aren't claims; answers are.

cards.headline: Why only claims count
cards.body: Level 2's arguments are built from statements: the reasons and the conclusion are all claims, because an argument tries to show that something is true. A command can't be a conclusion, since nothing could make "Wake up!" true. A claim can still join an argument when it turns out false. What matters is that asking "true or false?" makes sense.

cards.headline: Claims: sorted
learned: A claim is a sentence that can be true or false
A false claim is still a claim
Questions, commands and exclamations aren't claims
Premises and conclusions are always claims

questions.prompt: In logic, a sentence is a claim when _____.

options.label: it can be true or false
most people agree with it
options.rationale: Agreement doesn't matter; claims can be unpopular.

options.label: it is known to be true
it ends with a full stop

questions.explanation: A claim (or statement) is a sentence that can be true or false.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a claim?

options.label: Are you sleepy yet?
options.rationale: A question is neither true nor false.

options.label: Wake up!
options.rationale: A command is neither true nor false.

options.label: Ouch!
options.rationale: An exclamation is neither true nor false.

options.label: The Yangtze is a river in Japan.

questions.explanation: It's false, but it's still a claim: it's the kind of sentence that can be true or false.

questions.prompt: Why can't a command like "Wake up!" be the conclusion of an argument?

options.label: Commands are always too short
options.rationale: Length has nothing to do with it.

options.label: A conclusion must be something that could be true
Conclusions must already be known to be true
options.rationale: A conclusion only has to be able to be true or false.

options.label: Arguments can contain only one sentence
options.rationale: An argument needs at least two statements.

questions.explanation: An argument tries to show that something is true, so its conclusion must be a claim.
